title: Improving Writing Feedback for Struggling Writers: Generative AI to the Rescue?
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can support writing instruction by producing feedback and instructional suggestions for struggling writers. The authors focus on the practical question of how two versions of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) respond to student essays when prompted in different ways, and how those responses compare with teacher-generated rubric scores and instructional decisions.

The study used 34 persuasive essays written by students in grades 3–7 who were struggling writers, including students with high-incidence disabilities and English language learners. The essays came from an existing technology-based writing intervention that used a graphic organizer and embedded supports (WEGO/TBGO). The authors imported the essays into ChatGPT and ran four prompt types: a specific analytic rubric, a generic 0–4 rating, a request to identify one area of need without a rubric, and a general feedback prompt with no student context.

Across the generated responses, GPT-4 generally produced more specific and individualized feedback than GPT-3.5, while GPT-3.5 more often gave broad, misaligned, or repetitive feedback. Neither version reliably adapted feedback to student grade, disability status, or ELL status, and neither consistently produced instructional suggestions tailored to those characteristics. When compared with teacher judgments using the rubric, ChatGPT’s identification of the main area of need matched teacher decisions only modestly, though GPT-4 aligned better than GPT-3.5. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be useful as a starting point for feedback generation, but teacher review and judgment remain essential.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s conversational large language model chatbot used to generate and score writing feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Two versions of ChatGPT (GPT-3.5/free and GPT-4/subscription) were used to evaluate 34 student persuasive essays, generate formative feedback, identify areas of need, and suggest instructional responses under four prompt conditions.

findings.finding_summary: Using inductive thematic analysis of 34 persuasive essays, the study found that ChatGPT could generate rubric-based feedback and instructional suggestions, but output quality varied by version and prompt. GPT-4 was generally more specific and individualized than GPT-3.5, yet both versions produced excessive feedback, and neither consistently aligned suggestions with student characteristics such as grade, disability, or ELL status.
findings.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of AI-generated writing feedback and instructional suggestions

findings.finding_summary: Compared with teacher data-based decision making, GPT-3.5 matched the teacher-identified area of writing need 17.6% of the time and GPT-4 matched 23.5% of the time. For instructional decisions, GPT-3.5 yielded 26.5% partial matches and GPT-4 yielded 47.1% partial matches, indicating limited agreement and substantial need for teacher vetting before classroom use.
findings.measure: Agreement between teacher rubric-based decisions and ChatGPT-generated area-of-need labels and instructional suggestions

quality_tier_rationale: This is an original mixed-methods/qualitative secondary analysis of student writing and AI-generated feedback, not an RCT or meta-analysis. The study is useful for exploratory evidence but does not provide causal impact estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports practical promise, but the main quantitative agreement results are low-to-moderate and no effect sizes are reported. The findings suggest limited current classroom impact without teacher mediation.
